question:
Usain is walking for exercise by zigzagging across a \(100\)-meter by \(30\)-meter rectangular field, beginning at point \(A\) and ending on the segment \(\overline{BC}.\) He wants to increase the distance walked by zigzagging as shown in the figure below (\(APQRS\)). What angle \(\theta=\angle PAB\) \(=\angle QPC\) \(=\angle RQB=\cdots\) will produce a length that is \(120\) meters? (Do not assume the zigzag path has exactly four segments as shown; there could be more or fewer.)

[Figure 1](figures/2023_AMC_12A_Q15_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
The number of turns can stay unknown: every segment makes the same acute angle \(\theta\) with the forward direction along the field's 100-meter length.

[Figure 1](figures/2023_AMC_12A_Q15_question_fig1.svg)

Let the positive segment lengths be \(\ell_1,\ell_2,\ldots,\ell_k\), including the final segment ending on \(BC\). By the right-triangle definition of cosine, a segment of length \(\ell_i\) advances \(\ell_i\cos\theta\) in the direction of \(AB\).

Every segment moves forward, so these advances add to \(AB=100\). The total walking distance is \(120\), hence
\[
100=(\ell_1+\cdots+\ell_k)\cos\theta
=120\cos\theta.
\]
Therefore
\[
\cos\theta=\frac56,
\qquad \theta=\boxed{\arccos\frac56}.
\]
This is an acute angle, so the path can be continued forward, turning at the long sides until it reaches \(BC\). The calculation includes a final partial crossing and makes no assumption about the number of segments. The answer is choice \(\mathrm A\).

solutionMethods.explanation:
Reflecting the field at each turn turns the zigzag into one straight segment while preserving the distance walked.

At the first turn \(P\), reflect the remainder of the field and path across the long side through \(P\). Since the incoming and outgoing segments make equal angles with that side, the reflected outgoing segment continues straight along the incoming segment. Repeat this reflection at each later turn. Each reflection preserves lengths, so the resulting straight segment has length \(120\).

All reflections are across lines parallel to \(AB\), so they leave forward distances unchanged. The unfolded endpoint is therefore still \(100\) meters forward from \(A\), even when the last segment crosses only part of the field's width.

The unfolded segment makes angle \(\theta\) with the forward direction. In the resulting right triangle, its length \(120\) is the hypotenuse and its forward distance \(100\) is the adjacent leg. Thus
\[
\cos\theta=\frac{100}{120}=\frac56.
\]
The required acute angle is \(\boxed{\arccos\frac56}\), choice \(\mathrm A\). Folding the copies back produces the required path, regardless of how many long sides the straight segment crosses.
solutionMethods.label: Unfold the zigzag
